plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) serious warnings explained from the US label: the boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning and who shouldn't use it (personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2), pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney injury from fluid loss, severe allergic reactions, diabetic retinopathy (Mounjaro, type 2 diabetes), aspiration risk around anaesthesia, and the FDA's Nov 9, 2026 class-wide NAION eye warning, with how rare each one is
plan.angle: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) label warnings explained: what each one means, which signs need action, and how rare each one is where the label (or the FDA, for NAION) gives a rate. Use the current Zepbound PI (rev. 28 Aug 2026), the Mounjaro PI (rev. 27 Aug 2026) and the Medication Guide, each with its own URL. For NAION, use the FDA Drug Safety Communication of 9 Nov 2026 unless the PI fetched on publish day prints it. Keep the opening, the 15 s short answer and the second payoff as planned. Changes: (a) Thyroid chapter: in label wording, thyroid C-cell tumours were seen in rats and it is unknown whether tirzepatide causes them in humans, including MTC. Contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2. Give no human rate. (b) Kidney injury, serious allergic reactions and aspiration: say these come from post-marketing reports and the label gives no trial rate. Keep 'post-marketing' and the label's scope: acute kidney injury in the setting of fluid loss from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. (c) Pancreatitis, gallbladder, low blood sugar and retinopathy: use a rate only if it is printed with both arms and the exact trial population. Zepbound pooled = adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Mounjaro = type 2 diabetes trials. Never mix the two labels. Retinopathy is Mounjaro, type 2 diabetes only. Low blood sugar: higher risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea. (d) NAION: 'the FDA says there's a potential increased risk across GLP-1 medicines'. Pooled 126 trials: 6.4 vs 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years, GLP-1 medicines vs comparators, based on a small number of events. It wasn't shown for tirzepatide on its own, so never say 'causes'. Use the FDA's sign wording: sudden, often painless vision loss in one eye. Action: contact a healthcare professional right away, or your local urgent care or emergency number. Don't mention the providers' 'consider discontinuing' guidance as viewer advice. (e) Add one line saying the label lists other warnings too (severe GI disease, heart rate increase, mood changes and suicidal thoughts) and that the full list is in the Medication Guide. If mood or suicidal thoughts are mentioned, keep it calm, tell viewers to contact a healthcare provider right away, and give crisis resources for the US, UK, Canada and Australia, with no method detail. (f) Aspiration: the only action is 'tell your surgical and anaesthesia team that you take it'. Keep the scoped don't-stop line after the emergency signs, one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line, spoken and on screen. No dosing, titration, skipping or switching. Don't call NAION 'new' or 'this week'. Title: 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Serious Risks: How Rare?'. Thumbnail: 'HOW RARE?' with a carton and an unfolded leaflet, one calm labelled character, no body imagery.
plan.trend_stage: rising (FDA NAION label-change hook) on an evergreen label base
plan.why: Broad, steadily searched worry ('mounjaro thyroid cancer', 'zepbound warnings') with a peaking label-change hook, and almost all of it can be checked against the FDA label, so it should clear fact-check first time and keep earning search views. | fact-check: Good topic. It's a broad, searched label explainer in Lane A and doesn't break any ban, and the plan already handles the safety framing well. I checked the time-sensitive part. The FDA did issue a class-wide NAION Drug Safety Communication on 9 Nov 2026, requiring a Warnings and Precautions update for all GLP-1 RA medicines, including Mounjaro and Zepbound. The pooled FDA analysis covered 126 trials, 134,253 patients (78,217 on a GLP-1 RA, 56,036 on a comparator) and 288,879 patient-years. NAION rates were 6.4 per 100,000 person-years on GLP-1 RAs vs 3.8 on comparators, from 15 probable events: 10 on GLP-1 RAs, 5 on placebo and none on active comparators. Sources: Healio 2026-11-09, Ophthalmology Times, Optometry Times, Pharmacy Times, CNN 2026-11-09. Six changes are needed. (1) Use the exact printed figures, '6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years', not 'about 6 vs 4'. The FDA calls it a 'potential increased risk', so don't say tirzepatide causes NAION or that this was shown for tirzepatide specifically. These are pooled class data from very few events. The DSC tells providers to 'consider discontinuing' if NAION develops. That is clinician guidance and must not become viewer advice to stop. (2) The angle promises 'how rare each one is', but several warnings have no rate on the label. The thyroid C-cell tumour finding comes from rats and the human risk is unknown. Acute kidney injury and serious hypersensitivity reactions come from post-marketing reports. Aspiration comes from rare post-marketing reports. For these, say there's no trial rate on the label. Don't invent a rate or call one 'rare' unless the label does. (3) The title says 'Serious Risks', but the Zepbound label also lists severe GI disease, heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour and ideation. Don't present the 8 chapters as the complete list. Add a line that the full list is in the Medication Guide. If suicidal ideation is mentioned, it needs a calm, neutral line and crisis resources for all four markets, with no method detail. (4) Only use a rate if it is printed with both arms and the population. For the Zepbound pooled trials, name the population exactly: adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Study 1 excluded type 2 diabetes. The Mounjaro rates come from type 2 diabetes trials. Never combine numbers from the two labels. (5) Credit NAION to the FDA DSC with its date, unless the PI fetched on publish day prints it. Don't call it 'new' or 'this week', because the piece is evergreen. (6) The working title 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Serious Risks: How Rare?' is fine, because the video answers the question. The thumbnail 'HOW RARE?' is fine.

script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity: the viewer's exact question in sentence 1, the headline number (gallstones 1.1% vs 1.0%) by 15 s, a second payoff (the thyroid box comes from rats) by 30 s, then a 'you' kitchen-table scenario and one open loop (the FDA eye-warning numbers), paid off near the end

scenes.narration: Short answer: where the label prints a rate, the numbers are small. Take gallstones. One point one percent on tirzepatide. One percent on placebo.

scenes.narration: So what does a boxed thyroid warning actually mean for you?

scenes.narration: It sits in a black box at the very top of the label. It says that in rats, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumours.

scenes.narration: The label says it's unknown whether tirzepatide causes these tumours in humans, including a type called medullary thyroid carcinoma, or MTC.

scenes.narration: Why unknown? Because the human relevance of the rat tumours hasn't been determined. So there's no human rate to give you. Not rare, not common. Unknown.

scenes.narration: How often did pancreatitis actually show up in the diabetes trials?
Acute pancreatitis means sudden inflammation of the pancreas. The label notes it has been seen with GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines, including severe forms.
In Mounjaro's type 2 diabetes trials, confirmed acute pancreatitis came to zero point two three patients per hundred years of exposure on tirzepatide.

The Medication Guide says drinking fluids helps reduce your chance of dehydration. And if you can't keep fluids down, that's worth a call to your healthcare provider.

scenes.narration: Second, serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis and angioedema, which is swelling under the skin. The label describes post-marketing reports. scenes.narration: Why would your anaesthesia team care about a weekly injection?

The label says tirzepatide delays stomach emptying. Separately, it describes rare post-marketing reports of pulmonary aspiration in people on GLP-1 medicines under general anaesthesia or deep sedation.

scenes.narration: Pulmonary aspiration means stomach contents getting into the lungs. The people in those reports still had food in their stomach, despite reportedly following fasting instructions.

First, the Mounjaro label, for people with type 2 diabetes. Temporary worsening of diabetic retinopathy has been reported with rapid improvement in blood sugar control.

In plain English, it's a problem with blood flow to the optic nerve, the cable that carries signals from your eye to your brain.

scenes.narration: You may have heard of an older warning about depression and thoughts of suicide. In January 2026, after reviewing 91 trials, the FDA asked for it to be removed from the Zepbound label, because it found no increased risk. The FDA still says to tell your healthcare professional about new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, or any unusual changes in mood.

factcheck.summary: The science is accurate. Every number I checked matches its source: gallstones 1.1% vs 1%, inflamed gallbladder 0.7% vs 0.2%, acute kidney injury 0.5% vs 0.2%, severe allergic reactions 0.1% vs 0%, heart rate +1–3 bpm and GI events 'mostly during dose escalation' (Zepbound PI, Aug 2026). Pancreatitis is 0.23 vs 0.11 patients per 100 years of exposure (Mounjaro PI, Aug 2026). The FDA eye-condition (NAION) notice of 9 Nov 2026 gives 126 trials, 134,253 people, 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years, 15 probable cases and 'potential increased risk'. The FDA suicidality notice of 13 Jan 2026 covers 91 trials, removal from the Zepbound label and the mood-change advice. Label scopes stay correctly separated (Mounjaro = diabetes trials, Zepbound = weight trials), the slower stomach emptying is not stated as the cause of aspiration, emergency lines cover all four markets, and the don't-stop line comes after every warning sign. The hold-up is the source list. S2 (the Medication Guide) points to a URL that serves the Prescribing Information, and the PI doesn't contain the Medication Guide wording quoted in s24, s25, s29, s44 and s47. Swap in the working Medication Guide PDF. The other issues are wording polish.

issues.problem: When fetched, this URL returns the full Prescribing Information, which ends at section 17 and has no Medication Guide text. So the quoted 'stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away', 'drinking fluids helps reduce your chance of dehydration' and allergy/emergency wording (s24, s25, s29, s44, s47, s73, s78, s82) isn't backed by the listed URL. Craft rule: the Medication Guide needs its own working URL, never a PI anchor. The Medication Guide exists at Lilly's PDF URL, but the PDF wouldn't text-parse, so I couldn't confirm its wording or revision date.

In January 2026, after reviewing 91 trials, the FDA asked for it to be removed from the Zepbound label, because it found no increased risk. The FDA still says to tell your healthcare professional about new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, or any unusual changes in mood."

issues.problem: Accurate and correctly scoped. But the video's audience is mostly on weight treatment, and the Zepbound weight trials show no difference (0.2% in both groups; 0.14 vs 0.15 per 100 years of exposure). Showing only the diabetes pool makes the risk look like a doubling to that audience. This is optional balance, not an error.
issues.fix: Optionally add after s22: "In the Zepbound weight trials, it was about the same in both groups: zero point two percent on tirzepatide and on placebo." On-screen: "Zepbound weight trials: 0.2% vs 0.2%" (source S1).

hold_reason: Not rendered: Fact-checker verdict REVISE: The science is accurate. Every number I checked matches its source: gallstones 1.1% vs 1%, inflamed gallbladder 0.7% vs 0.2%, acute kidney injury 0.5% vs 0.2%, severe allergic reactions 0.1% vs 0%, heart rate +1–3 bpm and GI events 'mostly during dose escalation' (Zepbound PI, Aug 2026). Pancreatitis is 0.23 vs 0.11 patients per 100 years of exposure (Mounjaro PI, Aug 2026). The FDA eye-condition (NAION) notice of 9 Nov 2026 gives 126 trials, 134,253 people, 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years, 15 probable cases and 'potential increased risk'. The FDA suicidality notice of 13 Jan 2026 covers 91 trials, removal from the Zepbound label and the mood-change advice. Label scopes stay correctly separated (Mounjaro = diabetes trials, Zepbound = weight trials), the slower stomach emptying is not stated as the cause of aspiration, emergency lines cover all four markets, and the don't-stop line comes after every warning sign. The hold-up is the source list. S2 (the Medication Guide) points to a URL that serves the Prescribing Information, and the PI doesn't contain the Medication Guide wording quoted in s24, s25, s29, s44 and s47. Swap in the working Medication Guide PDF. The other issues are wording polish.
